newsitem.title: USA: Oklahoma bombing judge reinforces strong gag order.
newsitem.headline: Oklahoma bombing judge reinforces strong gag order.

text.p: The judge in the Oklahoma City bombing case Wednesday reinforced a strong gag order, prohibiting all attorneys in the case from making any statements outside the courthouse.

The judge's order follows by one day comments by chief defence attorney Stephen Jones on a new Justice Department study that said the FBI's crime laboratories provided flawed evidence in some major cases, including the Oklahoma City bombing.

Meanwhile, security remained tight as the second anniversary of the bombing approached. Some 70 miles (110 kilometres) south of Denver, NORAD and the U.S. Space Command announced that all public tours have been cancelled until further notice.

Barricades were placed outside its headquarters due to "possible security concerns," a spokeswoman said on Wednesday. But Franki Webster of the North American Aerospace Defence Command Centre declined to disclose the nature of the security concerns or say whether they were specifically related to the April 19 anniversaries of the 1995 Oklahoma City bombing and the 1993 federal siege of the Branch Davidian compound at Waco, Texas.

Just before the trial of accused bomber Timothy McVeigh opened on March 31, attorneys for both sides said the judge had told them to refrain from making comments as the jury selection process was at hand. Prosecutors have adhered to the order, although Jones continued to respond to journalists' questions.
McVeigh is charged with bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people. He has pleaded not guilty and faces the death penalty if convicted.
During pre-trial hearings last year and earlier this year prosecutors and defence attorneys used to sum up the day's proceedings for journalists.

Last June when he issued a partial gag order, U.S. District Court Judge Richard Matsch had specifically recognised the importance for McVeigh's lawyers to defend his interest in the "court of public opinion."

According to the judge's latest written order, those involved in the case are "prohibited from making any comments or statements outside the courtroom, concerning any of the evidence, court rulings and opinions regarding the trial proceedings and anything concerning the jury which a reasonable person would expect to be disseminated by any means of public communication."
The judge's three-page order also applied to McVeigh, law enforcement officials and all court personnel.

The trial is in its third week of jury selection. The judge noted that the jury will not be sequestered and that prospective jurors have been directed to avoid news accounts about the high-profile trial.

The judge said he has told jury candidates that journalists and commentators are not under any special rules of the court, but statements from the principal attorneys in the case may influence jurors.

"Any statements from the prosecutors, defence counsel, government officials and agents having responsibilities relevant to this case ... may reasonably be expected to be perceived differently (from news reports and analyses) and carry a much greater threat of prejudice to fairness," the judge wrote.

The judge, prosecutors and defence attorneys questioned six prospective jurors on Wednesday on a wide range of subjects, including the death penalty and how the bombing may have affected them. So far 79 potential jurors have been interviewed.
Among the interviewees were two grandmothers who said they were affected by the deaths of 19 children in the bombing and a cross-country skier who was on the junior U.S. Olympic team.

In his public comments on Tuesday, Jones said he expected the report on the Federal Bureau of Investigation crime lab to play some role in the trial, but that it was too early to say how important it would be.
